Philemon 1.summary: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, writes with Timothy to Philemon, his beloved fellow worker, together with Apphia, Archippus and the church that meets in Philemon's house (Philemon 1:1-3). He thanks God for what he hears of Philemon's love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and all the saints, prays that the sharing of Philemon's faith will be effective for a full knowledge of every good thing that is ours in Christ, and says Philemon's love has given him much joy and comfort because it has refreshed the hearts of the saints (Philemon 1:4-7). Although Paul could be bold enough to command, he chooses to appeal on the basis of love on behalf of Onesimus, whom he calls 'my child' and says he became a father to in his imprisonment (Philemon 1:8-10). Onesimus was formerly useless to Philemon but is now useful to both of them; Paul is sending him back, 'sending my very heart,' and says he would have liked to keep him but did not want to do anything without Philemon's consent, so that Philemon's goodness would be voluntary and not forced (Philemon 1:11-14). Paul suggests that Onesimus may have been parted from Philemon for a while so that Philemon might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother, both 'in the flesh and in the Lord' (Philemon 1:15-16). Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself, and says that if Onesimus has wronged him or owes anything, Paul will repay it, writing this promise in his own hand, while reminding Philemon that he owes Paul his very self (Philemon 1:17-20). Paul expresses confidence that Philemon will do even more than he asks, asks him to prepare a guest room because he hopes to visit, and closes with greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke and a blessing of grace (Philemon 1:21-25).
Philemon 1.whyItMatters: Knowing the legal and social power of slave owners in the Roman world shows how significant it was for Paul to ask a master to accept a slave as a brother and to avoid commanding him. At the same time, the gaps in the story remind readers to be careful not to claim more than the text says about Onesimus's past, about what Philemon did, or about Paul's view of slavery as an institution.
Philemon 1.whereWeAre:
Paul was in prison or chains when he wrote (1:1, 1:9, 1:10, 1:13, 1:23). The letter does not say why he was imprisoned. Acts 28:30-31 describes Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years.

Onesimus had become a believer through Paul, who calls himself his father in the faith, and was now with Paul. How he came to be there is not stated.

Slavery was widespread in the Roman Empire. Slaves were legally the property of their owners, who had wide authority over them. People became slaves through war, birth to enslaved mothers, debt or being abandoned as infants. Estimates of how many slaves there were vary widely among historians.

A slave who fled his master could be considered a fugitive, and owners could pursue and punish them harshly. Roman legal writings, however, also discuss the case of a slave who left his owner and took refuge with the owner's friend to ask him to intercede, and treat such a slave differently from a true fugitive (Digest 21.1.17.4). Some scholars apply this to Onesimus; the letter does not say.

A letter by the Roman writer Pliny the Younger (Letters 9.21, with the follow-up in 9.24), written about half a century later, asks his friend Sabinianus to forgive Sabinianus's own freedman, who had offended him. It shows that appeals on behalf of a wrongdoer by a third party were a recognized practice. Pliny's letter is not connected to Philemon, and it is a comparison and not a source.

Early Christian churches commonly met in private homes, and Philemon's house hosted such a gathering (1:2). Paul's appeal addresses a situation in which a slave owner had a Christian slave with possibly broken trust, in a society where owners had great legal power and shame could be attached to a slave's escape or wrongdoing. Paul does not ignore the social reality; he asks Philemon to treat Onesimus as a brother, putting the relationship in the framework of faith.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Writes the appeal, offers to repay any debt, and hopes to visit. His appeal models a pastoral approach based on love and personal cost.

keyFigures.name: Timothy
keyFigures.role: Named as a co-sender. Shows that Paul worked with a team.

keyFigures.name: Philemon
keyFigures.role: The person who must decide how to respond to Onesimus. The appeal depends on his character as described in 1:4-7.

keyFigures.name: Apphia
keyFigures.role: Named among the addressees. Shows that the letter was addressed to more than Philemon.

keyFigures.name: Archippus
keyFigures.role: Named among the addressees. Shows another member of the community with a ministry.

keyFigures.name: The church in Philemon's house
keyFigures.role: Included in the address. Suggests the letter was meant to be heard publicly.

keyFigures.name: Onesimus
keyFigures.role: The subject of the letter, who is being sent back. His change from 'useless' to 'useful' and from bondservant to brother is the heart of the letter.

keyFigures.name: God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Frame the greeting, the thanksgiving and the appeal 'in the Lord.' Paul grounds the appeal in their shared relationship to Christ.

keyFigures.name: The saints
keyFigures.role: Beneficiaries of Philemon's love. Shows the reputation on which Paul's appeal is based.

keyFigures.name: Epaphras
keyFigures.role: Sends greetings. Links the letter to the Colossian church.

keyFigures.name: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke
keyFigures.role: Send greetings. Show that Paul was with a group of co-workers.

keyFigures.name: Tychicus (background)
keyFigures.role: Possible carrier of the letter. Mentioned for background on how the letter may have reached Philemon; this is an inference from Colossians 4:7-9.

keyThemes.theme: Appeal grounded in love, not command
keyThemes.explanation:
Paul says he could be bold enough to command but prefers to appeal on the basis of love, and wants Philemon's goodness to be voluntary.

Christian love invites a free response rather than demanding obedience by force.

Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a bondservant but as a beloved brother, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

Shared faith changes how believers regard and treat one another, whatever their social status.

Paul offers to repay any debt Onesimus owes and signs it with his own hand.

Love can mean taking on the cost of reconciliation.

keyThemes.theme: Changed lives: from useless to useful
keyThemes.explanation:
Onesimus, once useless, is now useful, and has become Paul's child in the faith.

The gospel can change a person's character and standing in the community.

Paul thanks God for Philemon, prays for the sharing of his faith, and speaks of refreshing hearts and of partnership.

Hard conversations are best approached with gratitude and mutual trust.
